questions.q: How is the passive built in French?
choices: être + past participle, agreeing with the subject
questions.why: Être in any tense plus the participle: la maison est construite, a été construite, sera construite. The auxiliary carries the tense.

questions.q: Complete: « La maison a été ___ en 1920. » (construire)
questions.why: With être as auxiliary the participle behaves like an adjective and agrees with the subject: maison is feminine singular.

questions.q: « Le voleur a été arrêté ___ la police. »
questions.why: Par names the agent of an action. De is kept for a state or a feeling: il est respecté de tous.

questions.q: Complete: « Il est respecté ___ tous. » (by everyone)
questions.why: Respecter, aimer, admirer and other verbs of feeling take de rather than par, because the result is a state, not an event.

questions.q: Turn it into the passive: « La police a arrêté le voleur. »
questions.why: The direct object becomes the subject, avoir + participle becomes a été + participle, and the old subject follows par.

questions.q: Which is the natural French for « French is spoken here » ?
questions.why: When the agent is unnamed, French reaches for on with an active verb rather than a passive. The passive is heavy and mostly written.

questions.q: Which verb form goes with « on » ?
questions.why: On est là, on va partir, on a mangé — singular even when on plainly means we. Only a following participle may agree with the real meaning: on est allés.

questions.q: Translate with « on »: « I was told that he's leaving. » → « ___ m'a dit qu'il part. »
questions.why: French cannot promote an indirect object to subject, so there is no je suis dit. For I was told and he was given, on is the only option.

questions.q: Complete with a reflexive: « Comment ça ___ ? » (How is that spelled?)
questions.why: A reflexive verb is the natural passive when the subject is a thing and no agent matters: ça se dit, ce livre se vend bien.

questions.q: « Le vin blanc ___ frais. » (White wine is drunk chilled.)
questions.why: A general truth about a thing goes reflexive. Est bu is grammatical but sounds like a report of one specific glass.

questions.q: « Elle s'est ___ renverser par une voiture. »
questions.why: Se faire + infinitive is for something that happened to someone, usually unwelcome, and the participle fait is invariable there.
My car has been stolen. On here means someone, unidentified — one of its three uses alongside we and people in general.

questions.q: In « Nous, on préfère rester », what is « on » doing?
choices: it means we, with nous added for emphasis
it is a mistake for nous préférons
questions.why: In speech on has largely replaced nous as the subject, and nous can be tacked on in front purely for stress.

questions.target: il s'est fait voler son portefeuille
questions.why: He got his wallet stolen. Se faire + infinitive, with fait never agreeing.

questions.q: French has four ways to express an English passive. Name them and say when each is the right choice.
a: 1. The true passive, être + participle: use it when the agent matters (le livre a été écrit par Camus) or the register is formal or written (la décision a été prise). Par for an action, de for a feeling. 2. On + active verb: the default when there is no named agent, especially in speech — on a construit cette maison en 1920, on m'a dit que… It is also the only option when English promotes an indirect object (I was told, he was given a book). 3. A reflexive verb: for a general truth about a thing — ça se dit, ce livre se vend bien, comment ça s'écrit ? 4. Se faire + infinitive: for something, usually bad, that happened to someone — il s'est fait voler, je me suis fait avoir.
questions.why: Knowing the passive is for reading; knowing the three alternatives is what makes you sound French. On covers the largest share by far.
